newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Greenspan hails Conference Bd on anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Greenspan hails Conference Bd on anniversary.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan marked the Conference Board's 80th anniversary on Wednesday with words of praise for the non-profit research organization that gave him his first job in 1948.

"Much of my professional development, I trace back to those early days rummaging through a remarkable array of documents, books, statistics," Greenspan told a Conference Board's function. "What I learned during my five years at the Board proved invaluable in later life."

The National Industrial Conference Board was born in 1916 out of a somber page of American history when mines and factory workers protested -- violently at times -- against the very harsh conditions that shaped America's industrial development at the begining of the century.

Getting entrepreneurs to provide safe working conditions was a key concern of Board founder Magnus Alexander, an engineer with General Electric Co. who believed iron-fisted confrontations were an inefficient way to run a business.
Like Greenspan, Alexander believed in the merit of consensus.

"Although I had offers of employment at higher pay, it was an easy call to come work at a research operation with, perhaps, one of the best business-oriented libraries in the country," Greenspan said.

The Board's programs now encompass U.S. and international research, indices of business and consumer sentiment as well as issuing the Leading Indicators Index since the U.S. government decided to cut costs by privatizing an indicator.
One of very few women to be a chief economist on Wall Street is the Conference Board's chief economist Gail Fosler, also known in the marketplace as an excellent forecaster.
In June 1994, her forecast of a 10-percent dollar decline in the 18 months ahead was enough to depress dollar/mark by nearly three pfennigs to an eight-month low.
Fosler's forecast proved right as the dollar skidded from 1.63 marks in mid-June 1994 to end 1995 at 1.4330.

"Her forecast was driven purely by econometric analysis. The market's reaction had more to do with the respect people have for her -- because she is incredibly bright -- than for econometric modelling of the dollar," said analyst Kevin Harris at MCM CurrencyWatch.

The Board's most followed indicator is the monthly Consumer Confidence Index. In early 1996, Fosler relied on that index's high readings to issue a bullish U.S. 1996 growth forecast at a time when the Fed was lowering interest rates and many private analysts were warning of an impending recession.

Fosler correctly predicted the United States was heading for a consumer-led recovery, the Gross Domestic Product would rise by 2.6 percent in 1996, and the unemployment rate would stand at 5.4 percent by yearend.

"The confidence index is a highly useful survey of consumer sentiment and we use it frequently in trying to gauge the outlook for consumer spending, especially big-ticket items like cars and housing," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International.

Since 1972, the Board's consumer confidence index also proved to be a good gauge of voting intentions as every incumbent U.S. president has been reelected when that index topped a reading of 100. In September, consumer confidence stood at 111.8.
